newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada edges toward June federal election.
newsitem.headline: Canada edges toward June federal election.

text.p: It is just about as official as you can get -- an early June federal election is on everyone's mind in Ottawa even if Prime Minister Jean Chretien has not formally called one yet.

"There's a lot of momentum. All political parties are looking at the possibility, a very strong possibility, of an election in June," Defense Minister Doug Young said as he emerged from a Liberal caucus in Parliament on Thursday.

In Canada's British-style system, elections must be held every five years but the prime minister can call them anytime. The Liberals swept to an overwhelming majority in October 1993 in a backlash against the Conservatives of oft-reviled former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and Chretien appears to want another mandate while still fairly strong in the polls.
Polls show that if voter sentiment held he would win again, but his support has declined and he could have some tough fights on his hand, including for his own seat.

The Toronto Star and the Sun newspaper chain ran stories on Thursday saying their sources predicted Chretien would set a June 2 election, and the Star said he would call it on April 27, the latest date possible for a June 2 vote.

Teasing reporters, Chretien said on Thursday: "1997 is the year of the elections ... The question is should we have an election in June, or September or October." He said there would not be a decision for two or three weeks.

In a telling hint, the Quebec chapter of the Liberal Party just announced the postponement of its biennial convention -- scheduled for May 2-4 -- in case an election is called. The five main parties are holding nomination meetings daily in the 301 House of Commons districts to pick candidates, party headquarters are being opened or refurbished, and enumerators fanned out on Thursday to compile a voters list.

Liberal caucus leader Joe Fontana told reporters: "We're ready to go." Yet he cautioned that Chretien did have other considerations like trying to push through legislation such as an anti-tobacco bill that would die after an election call.

An Environics-Globe and Mail poll showed the Liberals with 47 percent of decided voters, followed by the Conservatives at 16 percent and 12 percent each for the leftist New Democrats, right-wing Reform and separatist Bloc Quebecois. This would give the Liberals between 178 and 222 seats, well over the 151 needed for a majority, and would return the Bloc to its role as the official opposition, the Globe said.

But 27 percent of those surveyed from March 11-31 were undecided, and pollsters caution that the Canadian electorate is increasingly volatile. They point to big swings in recent years once federal and provincial elections got under way.

An Angus Reid poll taken March 26-31 and released last week showed the Liberals at 41 percent, their lowest since being elected, followed by Reform at 19, Conservatives at 16, the Bloc at 14 and New Democrats at seven. With the Bloc and Reform concentrated in Quebec and the West, respectively, their threat is greater than the numbers show.

Analysts say a wild card will be how the Conservative and Reform pledges for broad tax cuts will resonate in view of the Liberal refusal so far to consider them before the deficit is licked -- and whether their platform will offer hope there.

The Liberals are also vulnerable on their right flank on social issues like gun control and gay rights. But in the biggest province, Ontario, pollsters say Reform and Conservative might well split the right-wing vote and allow the Liberals to take most seats, as in 1993.
On the left flank, the New Democrats are poised to make some inroads among voters unhappy with budget cuts.

The Environics polls covered 1,961 eligible voters and is considered accurate to within 2.2 percentage points 95 percent of the time. The Reid poll covered 1,500 people and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 points.
